strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem: reasoning models are decode-dominated, so calibrating pruning on prompt-only data creates a distribution mismatch that standard LLM pruning pipelines ignore.
Simple, practical, drop-in method (RAC) that integrates directly into existing pruning algorithms like SparseGPT without retraining or distillation.
Reasonably comprehensive experiments across four model scales (1.5B-32B), multiple sparsity levels (20-50%), and two task domains (math via MATH500, code via LiveCodeBench/CodeForces).
Useful mechanistic analysis (Figure 2, tokenwise reconstruction error heatmap) showing RAC specifically reduces error during the decode phase on held-out problems, supporting the core hypothesis.

Thoughtful ablations: on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, combination with semi-structured 2:4 sparsity and FP8 quantization, and the effect of maximum decode budget on runtime overhead, which nicely explains and partially resolves the counterintuitive 'pruning makes inference slower' phenomenon.
The runtime analysis is a distinguishing and practically relevant contribution beyond pure accuracy numbers, which many pruning papers ignore.
weaknesses: Only one base pruning algorithm (SparseGPT) is evaluated with RAC; despite claiming general applicability to WANDA/GPTQ-style methods, no experiments confirm this beyond a brief mention.

All experiments use a single model family (Qwen distilled from DeepSeek-R1); generality to other reasoning model architectures/training recipes (e.g., different distillation processes or natively RL-trained reasoning models) is untested.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental: it is essentially 'calibrate on self-generated rollouts instead of prompts only,' which is a reasonably natural extension of existing calibration-data literature (e.g., Bandari et al. 2024) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The added cost of generating full on-policy CoT rollouts (up to 8192 tokens) for calibration is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation without quantitative overhead reporting (e.g., wall-clock or GPU-hours compared to prompt-only calibration).

Some presentation/data issues: a missing dense baseline entry in Table 1 (32B, 50%, C4), a formatting typo in Table 3, and results discussion sometimes reads as a narrative restatement of table numbers rather than deeper analysis.

No comparison against alternative reasoning-aware compression baselines (e.g., PPC-GPT distillation-based approach mentioned in related work) to contextualize the magnitude of RAC's improvement relative to other reasoning-specific compression strategies.

The structured/quantization ablation (Table 4) is limited to a single model size (14B) and lacks error bars or repeated trials for throughput measurements, making claims about throughput gains less rigorously supported.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: compressing reasoning LLMs is understudied compared to compressing standard LLMs, and the paper correctly identifies that standard calibration (prompt-only) mismatches the decode-dominated nature of CoT inference.
The proposed fix (RAC) is simple and easy to integrate as a drop-in modification to existing one-shot pruning pipelines (e.g., SparseGPT) without requiring retraining or distillation.
Reasonably broad empirical sweep across model scales (1.5B-32B), sparsity levels (20-50%), and two task domains (math and code).

The tokenwise reconstruction-error heatmap (Figure 2) provides a nice mechanistic diagnostic showing that RAC specifically reduces error in the decode region on held-out problems, giving some qualitative insight beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
Several relevant ablations are attempted (on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, structured 2:4 sparsity + FP8 quantization, effect of test-time token budget).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the central idea (augment calibration data with self-generated/on-policy decode tokens) is a fairly direct combination of existing observations (Bandari et al. already show calibration data choice matters a lot; on-policy distillation is an established RL/LLM idea) rather than a substantively new technical contribution.

RAC is only demonstrated on top of a single pruning method (SparseGPT); despite claims that it 'integrates seamlessly into existing pruning workflows,' no experiments with WANDA, ALPS, or quantization-only baselines (e.g., GPTQ) are shown to support this generality claim.

The central motivating claim -- that pruning makes models slower via runaway CoT length, and that RAC fixes this -- is undercut by the paper's own Table 5: the RAC-pruned 40% model at 32k max tokens is both less accurate (91.2% vs 93.6%) and slower (29.1 vs 23.3 min) than the dense model, i.e., RAC does not clearly resolve the runtime pathology it uses to motivate the method; the 'fix' at smaller token budgets is really just capping generation length, not a consequence of RAC per se.

Many reported accuracy improvements are within one standard error of the baselines, particularly at lower sparsity levels (e.g., 14B/32B models at 20-30% sparsity), raising doubts about the statistical significance of the central claims; no significance testing or multiple-seed variance reporting is provided given the stochastic nature of on-policy rollout generation.

Evaluation is restricted to MATH500 and a code benchmark; there is no evaluation on other reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME, GPQA) or on general non-reasoning capabilities to check whether RAC calibration degrades broader model competence.

The computational overhead of RAC (collecting long on-policy CoT rollouts, up to 8192 tokens per calibration prompt, times M prompts and multiple sparsity levels) is acknowledged only qualitatively ('very modest') without concrete cost figures (GPU-hours, wall-clock time) compared to prompt-only calibration.

The paper's reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete abstract (the code link is missing/blank) and several bibliography/table errors (duplicate references for Frantar & Alistarh and DeepSeek-AI et al., a malformed entry in Table 3), suggesting insufficient polish.

Ablation results are incomplete/inconsistent, e.g., Table 4 is missing the 'Prompt+FP8, Entire Model' entry and the paper does not explain this gap, limiting the strength of the structured-pruning/quantization claims.

Limited exploration of the compression-accuracy Pareto frontier: only one quantization format (FP8) and one structured sparsity pattern (2:4) are tested, restricting the generality of the throughput claims.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a real, underexplored problem: standard LLM pruning calibration is prompt-centric, but reasoning models are decode-dominated, causing disproportionate accuracy loss and even inference slowdowns after pruning.

The proposed fix (RAC) is simple, well-motivated theoretically (matching calibration activation distribution to the on-policy decode-time distribution), and integrates as a drop-in replacement in existing one-shot pruning pipelines (e.g., SparseGPT) without retraining or distillation.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across model scales (1.5B to 32B Qwen/DeepSeek-R1-Distill models), two task domains (math via MATH500, code via LiveCodeBench/CodeGen), and several sparsity levels, showing consistent and sometimes large gains from RAC over C4 and prompt-only calibration, especially at high sparsity.

The tokenwise reconstruction-error analysis on held-out problems (Figure 2) provides a nice diagnostic that directly supports the paper's causal story—that RAC's advantage stems from better matching decode-time activations, not merely overlap with calibration data.

Useful ablations, including on-policy vs. off-policy CoT calibration, combination with structured 2:4 sparsity and FP8 quantization, and analysis of how bounding max decode length changes the runtime/accuracy tradeoff, which help contextualize when RAC's benefits matter most.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea is essentially changing the calibration corpus to include self-generated CoT rollouts, which is a natural, fairly predictable extension once the decode-dominated framing is stated (and related work such as Bandari et al. already shows calibration data choice matters greatly); no fundamentally new pruning objective or algorithm is proposed.

Evaluation is narrow in terms of pruning methods: only SparseGPT is evaluated in the main results, despite the paper mentioning WANDA and ALPS as being compatible; no results confirm RAC generalizes beyond one specific pruning algorithm.

Missing comparisons to other reasoning-aware or CoT-preserving compression baselines beyond the paper's own prompt-only/C4 ablations (e.g., no comparison with teacher-forced ground-truth CoT calibration instead of self-generated on-policy rollouts, which would isolate whether the gain comes from on-policy generation specifically or simply from including any long CoT-like text).

The calibration cost of on-policy rollout generation (which requires running full generation for every calibration prompt, potentially thousands of tokens) is acknowledged as a limitation but never quantified in wall-clock or compute terms, making it hard to assess the real practicality tradeoff versus prompt-only calibration.

Some result tables have gaps or inconsistencies (e.g., missing C4 result at 32B/50% sparsity without explanation, missing "Entire Model" column for Prompt+FP8 in Table 4), and gains at lower sparsity (20-30%) are often within or close to overlapping standard errors, making the practical significance of RAC less clear in the low-compression regime.

The reported reduction in runtime overhead is somewhat indirect and partially confounded: Table 5 shows that capping max decode length largely eliminates the runtime penalty for both dense and pruned models, suggesting much of the "RAC solves runtime" narrative in the abstract/intro is really about output-length capping rather than an intrinsic property of RAC.

Code generation accuracy is reported with a relatively lenient acc@1:16 metric (correct answer anywhere in top 16 predictions), which likely overstates robustness relative to a stricter pass@1 metric more standard in the literature, and no pass@1 results are given for code.

strengths: Identifies a clear and practically important failure mode: standard prompt-only calibration for pruning reasoning LLMs causes severe accuracy loss and can paradoxically increase inference latency due to longer, degenerate CoT traces at high sparsity.

The proposed fix (RAC) is simple, well-motivated theoretically (formalizes the mismatch between calibration activation distribution and true decode-time activation distribution), and integrates as a drop-in replacement into existing one-shot pruning pipelines (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS) without retraining.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple model families and sizes (DeepSeek-R1-distill Qwen 1.5B-32B, DeepSeek-R1-distill Llama 8B/70B, Qwen3 1.7B-14B), multiple sparsity levels, multiple benchmarks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), and multiple pruning algorithms, showing generally consistent gains from RAC especially at higher sparsity.

Useful ablations: on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, structured 2:4 pruning combined with FP8 quantization, effect of decode-length budget on runtime, and a token-wise reconstruction-error analysis on held-out problems that mechanistically supports the claimed benefit of RAC during the decode phase.

Clear and reasonably rigorous positioning against related work (concurrent benchmarking study, self-calibration, calibration-dataset studies), correctly distinguishing RAC's use of task-conditioned on-policy CoT activations from prior approaches.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental relative to existing self-calibration approaches (Williams et al., 2025) and prompt-only calibration baselines already tested in this paper; the contribution is largely combining/extending known ideas (on-policy generation, CoT-aware calibration) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The paper does not quantify the additional computational cost of collecting on-policy CoT activations (which requires full autoregressive rollouts up to 8192 tokens per calibration prompt) relative to standard single-pass prompt calibration; this is asserted to be 'modest' without supporting numbers, which is important since decode is far more expensive than prefill.

Benchmarks used for fine-grained comparisons (MATH500 with 500 problems, AIME-25 with only 30 problems) yield large standard errors, and many reported differences between RAC and baselines—particularly at lower sparsity levels (20-30%)—fall within overlapping confidence intervals, raising questions about the statistical robustness of some claimed improvements.

Results appear to be based on a single pruning/calibration run per configuration (no repeated calibration seeds or multiple pruning masks reported), limiting the ability to assess variance introduced by the pruning process itself as opposed to evaluation noise.

Some presented results are not fully explained or are internally inconsistent (e.g., Table 6 structured-pruning+quantization results show accuracy dropping noticeably for 'Entire Model' RAC+FP8 despite higher throughput, and several missing values/baselines are not discussed).

No comparison to alternative or complementary efficiency approaches for reasoning models (e.g., distillation-based shortening of CoT, speculative decoding, or learned length control) that could contextualize how competitive one-shot pruning with RAC is against other deployment-cost-reduction strategies.

Reproducibility details are somewhat sparse (e.g., exact number of calibration prompts/CoT samples per model, compute budget for RAC's activation collection phase, and hyperparameters for baselines like ALPS/WANDA) and code is only promised, not verifiable at review time.

strengths: The core problem being addressed (reasoning LLMs are decode-dominated, so prompt-only calibration misaligns with inference-time activation distributions) is well-motivated and clearly articulated.
The method (RAC) is simple, drop-in, and model/pruning-algorithm agnostic, demonstrated with SparseGPT, WANDA, and ALPS.
Broad experimental coverage across model families (DeepSeek-R1-Distill Qwen/LLaMA, Qwen3) and sizes (1.5B-70B), multiple benchmarks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), and multiple sparsity levels.
Several useful ablations are included: on-policy vs off-policy CoT source, structured 2:4 sparsity + FP8 quantization, varying max decode budget, and varying the pruning backbone algorithm.
The qualitative reconstruction-error heatmap (Figure 2) provides some mechanistic insight into why RAC helps specifically during the decode phase.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially replacing/augmenting calibration tokens with model-generated continuations, which is conceptually very close to prior 'self-calibration' work (Williams et al., 2025) and prompt-conditioned calibration (PPC-GPT); the distinguishing details (conditioning on task prompts, decode-only emphasis) are relatively incremental rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Statistical reliability is a serious concern: many reported improvements fall within overlapping standard errors (e.g., Table 1 7B at 20-30% sparsity, Table 4 AIME-25 results), yet the paper repeatedly claims RAC 'consistently' and 'substantially' outperforms baselines without any significance testing. AIME-25 has only ~30 problems, giving SEs of 0.08-0.09, making many comparisons essentially noise.

Several results are implausible or under-explained: pruned models sometimes outperform the dense baseline (e.g., Qwen3-8B at 30% sparsity: 0.972 vs 0.962 dense; DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-32B at 20% sparsity: 0.950 vs 0.942 dense), which is not discussed and raises concerns about evaluation noise, calibration/eval overlap, or data leakage (calibration uses OpenR1-Math-220K prompts — no analysis of overlap with MATH500/AIME-25 test sets is provided).

Runtime claims are central to the paper's motivation but the measurement methodology (batch size, hardware utilization, whether timings include evaluation harness overhead) is not described in sufficient detail for reproducibility, and some tables have missing dense baselines for runtime (e.g., Table 5), undermining direct verification of the central 'pruning slows inference' claim.

Practical significance of unstructured pruning results is questionable since unstructured sparsity rarely yields real hardware speedups without specialized kernels; the more practically relevant structured 2:4 experiments (Table 6) are limited to a single model/benchmark and contain incomplete entries (missing Prompt+FP8 'Entire Model' result).

No comparison against even lightweight retraining/fine-tuning baselines (e.g., short LoRA recovery after pruning) to contextualize how much of the dense-model gap remains with one-shot RAC versus cheap recovery alternatives.

The paper does not quantify the additional compute/time cost of RAC's calibration-time autoregressive rollout generation (beyond a vague 'modest' claim in the limitations), which matters since decode-time activation collection for 8192-token CoTs across many prompts could be substantial relative to standard calibration.

The comparison to the closest related work (Zhang et al., 2025b) is only framed as 'concurrent,' and no direct head-to-head experiment under matched settings is provided to isolate the specific contribution of injecting CoT activations versus other confounds (e.g., dataset domain match).

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an overlooked issue in compressing reasoning LLMs: standard pruning calibrates on prompt tokens, which mismatches the decode-dominated nature of CoT generation, and convincingly shows this causes severe accuracy loss and even runtime blow-ups (longer rambling CoTs).
The proposed fix (RAC) is simple, theoretically well-motivated, and drop-in compatible with existing one-shot pruning pipelines (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS) without requiring retraining/distillation.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple model families (DeepSeek-R1-Distill Qwen/LLaMA at several scales 1.5B-70B, Qwen3 1.7B-14B), multiple benchmarks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), multiple sparsity levels, and multiple pruning algorithms, with consistent and often large gains from RAC over C4 and prompt-only calibration.

Thoughtful set of ablations: on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, structured 2:4 sparsity + FP8 quantization combined with RAC, effect of maximum decode budget on runtime, and a token-wise reconstruction-error analysis on held-out problems that mechanistically supports the claimed benefit of RAC during the decode phase.

Practical framing: all experiments run in single-GPU, one-shot setting, which is realistic given that full retraining pipelines for reasoning models are often unavailable; the paper also shows that controlling max decode length mitigates most of the runtime penalty, providing actionable guidance.
weaknesses: The core idea (using model/domain-specific generated or self-generated text instead of generic C4 as calibration data) is a natural, fairly incremental extension of existing lines of work (Bandari et al. 2024 on calibration data choice; self-calibration by Williams et al. 2025), and the technical novelty is primarily the specific application to on-policy CoT traces rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Calibration-time cost of RAC (generating up to 8192 on-policy decode tokens per calibration prompt across potentially many prompts) is non-trivial and only briefly acknowledged in the limitations without quantitative comparison to prompt-only or C4 calibration overhead.

Some reported results show instability or missing entries (e.g., '–' at high sparsity for C4, 0.000 accuracy on AIME-25 for some configurations), and no multiple-seed/pruning-run variance is reported—only benchmark-level standard errors are shown, leaving open how sensitive RAC's benefits are to calibration sampling noise.

The method implicitly assumes access to task-relevant prompts (e.g., OpenR1-Math, Codeforces) for calibration, which may limit applicability to more general-purpose reasoning deployment scenarios where the downstream task distribution is unknown or more diverse than math/code.

Comparisons to alternative compression approaches beyond pruning (e.g., low-rank compression, distillation-based compression, or structured pruning methods beyond 2:4) are limited, and the structured-pruning/quantization results (Table 6) have incomplete entries, reducing confidence in generality of throughput claims.

The paper does not explore or discuss failure modes of RAC itself (e.g., whether it could overfit to the specific CoT style of the calibration prompts, hurting generalization to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks not represented in calibration data).
